questions.help:
Safe driving      
     
5 Driving in rain
5.1.1 Aquaplaning
Aquaplaning (also referred to occasionally as ‘hydroplaning’) is a frightening phenomenon whereby a wedge (or film) of water builds up between the tyres and the road surface. The depth of water on the road may be excessive for the grooves of the tyre to suitably displace it, which may also be heightened because of an inadequate depth of tyre tread.  
This causes the vehicle to feel like it is “gliding or sliding on the water”. The result is complete loss of normal control by the driver.
(Página 228 del manual 'Learning to drive')

Safe driving      
       
5 Driving in rain
5.1.1 Aquaplaning
Aquaplaning is caused by the accumulation of water on the road and by irregularities in its surface. Therefore, when it rains, it is necessary to pay special attention to potholes and areas in which puddles may occur.
This effect is more likely to occur with inappropriate speed and very wide or badly worn tyres.
One of the best solutions to avoid aquaplaning is to reduce the speed in the first instance, so that the tyres can displace the water and the wheels can retain contact with the road surface.
(Página 228 del manual 'Learning to drive')

Specifically, it is prohibited to overtake:
In any place or circumstance where visibility is not sufficient to be able to complete the manoeuvre or abort it once started, unless the two directions of traffic are clearly marked out and the manoeuvre can be completed without moving into the zone reserved for the opposite direction, specifically:

- When the weather conditions significantly reduce visibility (fog, heavy rain or when the sun is low, dazzling drivers). In these circumstances, you should never overtake.

questions.help:
Road traffic collisions  
   
1 A public health problem
Moreover, in addition to the human drama, it is important to highlight the enormous economic impact (either directly or indirectly) that occurs as a result of a traffic collision.
Costs derived from road traffic accidents are classified as human, material, healthcare and administrative.
Human costs include the loss of lives, productive capacity and physical and psychological suffering. Material costs consist of damages caused on vehicles and their loads as well as on the road and the environment. Healthcare costs comprise first aid, care and treatment of the wounded, rehabilitation and adaptations. Administrative costs hold those of police officers and firefighters and insurance and services management.
People believe that an accident has little effect on them but the cost is borne by taxpayers. The cost of vehicle insurance is also affected, as premiums are affected by collision data and the cost of accidents.
For these reasons, various international organisations, including the World Health Organisation (WHO), believe that road collisions are a priority public health problem throughout the world.
There is a serious need to work together to reduce the high numbers of dead and seriously injured on the roads.
(Página 248 del manual 'Learning to drive')

5.2.1 Order of preference in the absence of road signs
The following explains the order of preference in the absence of road signs, signals or authorised persons, and applies to priority when different types of vehicles approach a narrow road section and it is necessary for one of the vehicles to reverse back to allow the other vehicle to pass. Under these circumstance priority is given as follows:
1.Special vehicles and those travelling under special regulations that exceed the established masses and dimensions as per the regulated rules of vehicles (MAM).
2. Set of vehicles-except those within point 4 below.
3. Vehicles pulled by animals.
4. Cars that tow a trailer of up to 750 kilograms MAM and camping vehicles.
5.Public transport vehicles-designed to transport passengers.
6. Lorries, tractive units and good vans and goods vehicles.
7. Car and vehicles derived from cars.
8. Special vehicles that do not exceed the mass or dimension established within the regulating laws; heavy quadricycles and light quadricycles.

questions.help:
12 Distances
 
12.2 The braking distance
The braking distance is the distance the vehicle travels from the point at which the driver first applies the brakes, until the vehicle come to a complete stop.
This distance can vary depending on:
The speed of the vehicle at the point the brakes are applied.
The mass of the vehicle and its load.
The technical condition of the vehicle (brakes, tyres, shock absorbers, etc.)
The environmental conditions and the condition of the road surface (snow, rain, state of the surface, etc.)
The driver (psychophysical status –mental and physical state, experience, etc.)
An increase in speed causes the braking distance to increase, but this is at a greater rate than the speed increase.
Thus, when the velocity is doubled the braking distance is four times higher.
(Página 179 del manual 'Learning to drive')

questions.help:
ACTIVE SAFETY FEATURES      
       
4 Wheels    
4.2 Tyres  
4.2.2 Tyre markings
The sides of the tyres contain information relating to their characteristics. The main ones are:
It is prohibited to mount tyres with a load index or a code below the speed of the tyres that were originally mounted on the vehicle or as recommended by the manufacturer. However, you can mount tyres that are greater than those recommended.
Type of tyres: At present, most tyres are tubeless.
Date of manufacture: Identifies the date of manufacture of the tyre by the use of four digits. The first two represent the week of the year and the last two the year of manufacture. For example, “1520” means week 15 (mid-April) of 2020. These figures may be within an oval.
Location indicator for wear: Tread wear indicators can be found within the grooves of the tyre. Tyre manufacturers mould tread wear indicators (T.W.I) into the design of the tyres tread pattern. This may be indicated by the symbol TWI (Tread Wear Indicator), or a triangle, arrow or other symbol indicated by the manufacturer.
(Página 69 del manual 'Learning to drive')

questions.help:
Road traffic collisions    
     
RISK GROUPS    
5 Pedestrians
5.1 Children
Some of these limitations of children are:
Limiting the field of vision. When a child walks between parked cars the visual field can become 40% lower than that of an adult, due to their short stature. In addition, they also have problems with peripheral vision, which requires them to turn their head in order to see properly.
Hearing problems. The under seven’ are not adequately able to locate sound by direction, so they have problems locating a vehicle and judging the direction it is approaching from. This requires the child to look both ways and to turn their head in order to locate the sound.
(Página 252 del manual 'Learning to drive')

questions.help:
DISTRACTIONS        
     
5 Collisions due to distractions
To drive safely requires the driver to focus all of their attention on driving. Diverted attention results in the driver not receiving all of the necessary information on time, which ultimately leads to wrong decisions or delayed reactions.
Distractions can be caused by internal factors within the vehicle (such as GPS or smoking), or by external elements (such as advertising, road works or the views and landscape). Additionally, the driver may become distracted due to his state or mind (for example, preoccupied due to work).
(Página 33 del manual 'Learning to drive')
